title: Shellfish in pregnancy: cooked shrimp, crab, and what to skip
excerpt: Shrimp, crab, clams, and squid are FDA/EPA Best Choices when fully cooked. Skip raw shellfish and cold prawns that have not been reheated.
content:
## Overview

Shellfish is not banned in pregnancy. The split that matters is **fully cooked** versus **raw or eaten cold**. FDA and EPA list shrimp, crab, lobster, clams, oysters, scallops, and squid as Best Choices — the lower-mercury group — inside the weekly amounts on their fish chart. The NHS lists cooked prawns, crab, lobster, squid, mussels, scallops, clams, and cockles as foods that are safe to eat. The same agencies say to avoid raw shellfish, raw sushi, and sashimi.

This article does not say a single raw oyster is fine. Raw is the part to skip, even when the species is low in mercury.

## What the mercury chart says about shrimp and crab

FDA and EPA advise people who are pregnant or breastfeeding to eat 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list, **or** 1 serving from the Good Choices list and no other fish that week. One serving on the chart is 4 ounces, about 113 g, weighed before cooking. Across the week, the Best Choices path is about 8 to 12 ounces (about 225–340 g) of lower-mercury seafood. On a home plate, a cooked portion of about 90–120 g is a realistic serving for one adult — close to that pre-cook size after cooking loss, not a symbolic 30 g piece.

Shrimp, crab, clams, oysters, scallops, lobster, and squid appear on the FDA Best Choices list. They are not on the Choices to Avoid list (swordfish, shark, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, bigeye tuna). Rotating a few Best Choices species is better than eating the same species at every meal.

If you already ate one Good Choices serving this week (some albacore tuna meals fall here), FDA says not to add other fish that week. Do not treat shrimp as “not counting” so you can exceed that limit.

The NHS states the idea differently, and the numbers are not the same: about 2 portions of fish a week, a portion around 140 g, and no more than 2 portions of oily fish (salmon, trout, mackerel, sardines, herring). Prawns and crab are not on that oily-fish list. The NHS tuna limit is separate (not more than 4 cans or 2 tuna steaks a week). When the two systems differ, follow the clinician who is actually caring for you. Do not add the US ounces to the UK portions and invent a third limit.

Seafood caught by family or friends may not match the commercial chart. Check the local advisory before eating fish or shrimp from a private catch.

## Cook until the flesh is opaque and the shells open

CDC places raw fish and shellfish — including sashimi, raw sushi, and ceviche — on the riskier side of its pregnancy chart. The safer side: fish cooked to 145°F (63°C) or until the flesh is opaque and separates with a fork; shellfish cooked until the shells open during cooking, or until the flesh is pearly or white and opaque. For live oysters, CDC says to boil for another 3 to 5 minutes after the shells open. Discard shellfish that stay closed. Do not pry them open and eat them.

The NHS avoid list includes raw fish, raw shellfish, and sushi made with raw fish even if it was previously frozen. Freezing does not make raw sushi a safe pregnancy choice under that NHS wording.

In the kitchen:

- Steamed, stir-fried, or simmered shrimp: done when the shell is red and the flesh is opaque, not translucent.
- Stir-fried or steamed crab: meat set, with no raw patches at the joints.
- Clams, cockles, and mussels: shells open as they steam; throw away any that stay shut.
- Stir-fried or steamed squid: opaque flesh. Squid salad and squid sashimi are foods to skip.
- Seafood hot pot: the pieces need long enough in boiling broth to cook through, not a quick rare dip.

A single cooked portion of about 90–120 g fits one person, inside the weekly seafood amount of whichever chart you are following.

## Cold prawns and smoked seafood

Cooking once and then chilling the food does not automatically make it safe to eat cold. The NHS puts cold, pre-cooked, ready-to-eat prawns in the “be careful” group and says they must be cooked until steaming hot. A plate of boiled shrimp from the fridge — summer rolls, salad, a sandwich — should be reheated until steaming, or replaced with shrimp just cooked.

CDC also places refrigerated smoked seafood, unless it is part of a cooked dish, on the riskier side. Dried squid as a snack is not that smoked-refrigerated category, and it is also not the hot cooked protein of a main meal. If a seafood product is smoked and sold refrigerated, use the smoked-seafood caution.

Canned fish and shellfish in sealed cans are listed by CDC as a safer choice than refrigerated smoked fish. Still choose lower-mercury species and count them in the weekly servings.

## Vietnamese-style plates

- Rice, fully simmered shrimp, stir-fried morning glory, and sour soup that boiled (sprouts only if they stayed in the boiling pot until soft, not scattered on raw at the table).
- Hot seafood noodle soup with shrimp and squid cooked before serving, plus washed herbs. Do not set it up so people dip raw pieces.
- Lemongrass steamed clams, eating only the ones that opened, with a modest dip if you are watching salt or blood pressure.

Skip raw oysters, shrimp salad, raw clam salad, sashimi, and cold shrimp that has not been reheated. Fish sauce and table salt stay modest. Iodine from seafood and from iodized salt is a separate nutrition topic, not a reason to make the dipping sauce very salty.

If you already know you are allergic to shrimp or crab, leave the whole group out. Fully cooked eggs, lean cooked meat, beans, and tofu cover protein instead. Do not test “just a little” during pregnancy.

## If you do not eat seafood

FDA notes that fish provide protein, omega-3 fats, and several micronutrients, and also notes that people can meet needs with other foods if they do not eat the suggested servings. Do not buy a high-dose fish oil on your own to “catch up.” Ask your clinician before a DHA capsule or cod-liver oil. Products differ, and high-dose retinol vitamin A is a separate problem.

A vegetarian pattern still needs a plan for iron, vitamin B12, iodine, and choline with the prenatal clinician. It is not solved by deleting shrimp from a menu.

## When to seek care

Illness after seafood — vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, rash, trouble breathing, or swollen lips — needs emergency care if allergy signs are severe, or a call to maternity care if the problem is vomiting and diarrhea during pregnancy. Eating a clam that never opened, or a raw oyster, is worth telling your clinician about if you later develop a fever or cannot keep fluids down.

Educational only. The FDA/EPA chart and the NHS list do not replace personal advice if you have liver disease, a known allergy, or a prescribed diet.

faqs.question: Can pregnant people eat shrimp?
faqs.answer: Yes when the shrimp is fully cooked and counted in the week’s lower-mercury seafood. FDA and EPA list shrimp as a Best Choice. Cold boiled shrimp should be reheated until steaming hot, which is the NHS caution for ready-to-eat prawns.

faqs.question: Are raw oysters safe because they are low in mercury?
faqs.answer: No. Oysters are a Best Choice for mercury, but CDC and NHS both say to avoid raw shellfish. Eat them only fully cooked, shells open, and for live oysters follow the extra boil after they open.

faqs.question: How much shellfish belongs in a week?
faqs.answer: FDA/EPA: 2 to 3 Best Choices servings, about 4 ounces (113 g) each before cooking, or 1 Good Choices serving and no other fish that week. The NHS uses portions around 140 g and a separate oily-fish limit. Follow the clinician caring for you.
